<reason>PRO (Side B) won by holding the motion to its actual comparison — short-form/creator work versus traditional channel expansion — and forcing CON to concede most of the load-bearing claims (the young live in feeds, the newsroom should make clips for feeds, nobody should launch new linear channels). CON's strongest surviving line was "order" and attribution collapse, delivered with memorable rhetoric ("be indispensable first, then be everywhere"), but CON never defended channel expansion itself, instead substituting owned apps, sports rights and drama — a third option outside the motion's comparison. CON's charge that PRO won a "phantom" motion was undercut by PRO's unrebutted BBC Three relaunch example, and CON's closing attack that PRO accepts "relevance even if she never learns who made it" mischaracterised B4.5, which explicitly said the content carries the broadcaster's name. PRO answered both pressure questions with clear A1/A2 labels, named the loser plainly (expansion), and honestly declined to fabricate a funnel statistic while offering a directional mechanism. CON's answers were also well-labelled and its Q1 pressure was genuinely sharp, but PRO's reply — that existing services are commitments the motion never ranks — was faithful to the text. Clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's second rebuttal and closing turning CON's own words back ([A4.3] "clips of that work, posted where she is"; [A4.4] "the newsroom makes it, published in the feeds"; [A4.7] "nobody is launching channels") to show CON had adopted every premise of the motion and was left contesting only "order" — then answering that "afterthought clips get skipped, native ones get watched."</best_rebuttal>
